title: 36. Effect of lupin grain processing as a supplement during winter backgrounding of grazing beef calves.
content:
Abstract
Lupin grain (Lupinus angustifolius) has shown consistent productive responses when used as an energy–protein supplement in winter grazing backgrounding systems for beef calves. However, mechanical processing of the grain involves additional costs and greater operational complexity, making it relevant to evaluate its necessity under grazing conditions. This study evaluated the effect of supplementing whole or cracked lupin grain on average daily gain (ADG) and supplement feed conversion efficiency (SFE) of beef calves grazing winter pasture during a 70-day period. Thirty-six Hereford calves (159 ± 15.5 kg body weight, BW) were randomly assigned to one of three treatments: grazing Italian ryegrass without supplementation (CON), grazing Italian ryegrass supplemented daily with whole lupin grain (WL), or cracked lupin grain (CL), both offered at 1 kg dry matter (DM) per 100 kg BW. All treatments were managed under a restricted forage allowance of 2.5 kg DM per 100 kg BW in independent weekly plots (n = 3 plots per treatment; 4 calves per plot). Body weight was recorded every 14 days. Supplement DM intake was measured daily as the difference between the amount offered and refusals, and SFE was calculated as kilograms of supplement DM consumed per kilogram of additional BW gain relative to CON. Pasture biomass and sward height were measured weekly before and after grazing to adjust forage allowance and estimate forage utilization. Data were analyzed using a completely randomized design, and orthogonal contrasts were used to evaluate the effect of supplementation (CON vs. WL + CL) and lupin grain processing effects (CL vs. WL). No differences were observed in pre-grazing pasture biomass or sward height among treatments (2644 ± 177 kg DM/ha and 20.4 ± 0.6 cm, respectively; P > 0.05). Supplementation reduced forage utilization compared with CON (55.6 and 53.6 vs. 68.8% for WL, CL, and CON, respectively; P < 0.01), resulting in greater post-grazing biomass and residual sward height, with no differences between whole and cracked lupin grain. Supplementation with lupin grain increased ADG compared with CON (0.84 and 0.94 vs. 0.44 kg/d for WL, CL, and CON, respectively; SE: 0.07; P < 0.0001; Table 1). No significant differences in ADG were detected between whole and cracked lupin grain (P > 0.05). Total DMI (kg DM/100 kg BW) was greater in supplemented treatments than in CON (2.34 and 2.27 vs. 1.73 for WL, CL, and CON, respectively; SE: 0.07; P = 0.0007). Supplement feed conversion efficiency was similar between WL and CL (4.54 vs. 3.92 kg DM/kg additional BW gain; SE: 0.59; P > 0.05). Overall, these results indicate that lupin grain supplementation improves winter growth performance of grazing beef calves and that mechanical processing of the grain is not required under the evaluated conditions.
